lead: This unit is about separating a solute from a fluid by sticking it to a solid (adsorption), swapping ions on a resin (ion exchange), forming pure crystals from solution (crystallization), and separating water or ions with membranes. After it, you can size an adsorber from isotherm data, read a breakthrough curve, compute ion-exchange capacity, build a crystallization yield and heat balance, and predict crystal size distribution for an MSMPR crystallizer.
about: Unit 6 has nine chapters. 6.1 introduces adsorption and adsorbents. 6.2 gives the Langmuir and Freundlich isotherms. 6.3 moves to batch and fixed-bed adsorbers and breakthrough curves. 6.4 applies the same column thinking to ion exchange. 6.5 starts crystallization with solubility and supersaturation. 6.6 explains nucleation and growth. 6.7 classifies crystallizers and does yield and heat balances. 6.8 predicts crystal size distribution with the MSMPR model. 6.9 closes with reverse osmosis, electrodialysis and ultrafiltration. The first four chapters build on mass-transfer coefficients and stage ideas from earlier units; the last five connect equilibrium, kinetics and equipment design. The sequence moves from a single particle to a column, then to a crystal and a crystallizer, and ends with membrane modules.

chapters.idea: Adsorption holds solute molecules on the surface of a porous solid; the solid's area and pore structure set its capacity.
chapters.depth: Cover physical vs chemical adsorption, physisorption vs chemisorption, adsorbate and adsorbent terms, surface area, pore size, and common adsorbents: activated carbon, silica gel, alumina, zeolites, and ion-exchange resins as a bridge. Show why high area and small pores help. Some syllabi call physical adsorption van der Waals adsorption. Keep isotherm mathematics to 6.2.

figure.title: Adsorption path
figure.aria: A right-going block flow from feed through film diffusion and pore diffusion to surface adsorption, then to treated fluid; the adsorption site is highlighted.

chapters.example: 2.00 g activated carbon is shaken with 100 mL of dye solution. Initial dye concentration 50 mg/L; final 10 mg/L. Find adsorption capacity q in mg/g. q = (C0 - Ce)V/W = (50 - 10) mg/L × 0.100 L ÷ 2.00 g = 2.0 mg/g.
chapters.trap: Using solution volume in mL with mg/L, or forgetting to convert 100 mL to 0.100 L.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 diffusion for pore transport; Unit 2 interphase transfer.
chapters.leave: Isotherm equations to 6.2; fixed-bed breakthrough to 6.3; membrane surface transport to 6.9.

chapters.idea: Equilibrium adsorption at a fixed temperature is summarised by an isotherm linking q, the solid loading, to C, the fluid concentration.
chapters.depth: Langmuir: q = qmax K_L C/(1+K_L C); define qmax (monolayer capacity, mg/g) and K_L (affinity, L/mg). Freundlich: q = K_F C^(1/n); define K_F and n. Show linear forms and how to plot constants. Temperature rise lowers physisorption; pressure rise raises gas loading. Mention favourable isotherms.

figure.title: Langmuir isotherm and worked points
figure.aria: A rising Langmuir curve that flattens near 40 mg/g, with two marked points at Ce 2 mg/L and q 30 mg/g and at Ce 0.667 mg/L and q 20 mg/g.

chapters.example: At 25 °C, a dye on activated carbon follows the Langmuir isotherm with qmax = 40 mg/g and K_L = 1.5 L/mg. (a) Find q at Ce = 2.0 mg/L. (b) Find Ce when q = 20 mg/g. (a) q = 40 × 1.5 × 2.0 ÷ (1 + 1.5 × 2.0) = 120 ÷ 4 = 30 mg/g. (b) 20 = 60 Ce ÷ (1 + 1.5 Ce), so 20 + 30 Ce = 60 Ce and Ce = 0.667 mg/L.
chapters.trap: Using the Langmuir linear plot and taking the intercept as qmax instead of 1/qmax; mixing C units with q units.
chapters.leave: Batch contact time to 6.3; ion-exchange selectivity to 6.4.

chapters.idea: A fixed bed adsorbs well until a mass-transfer zone reaches the exit; the breakthrough curve records that arrival.
chapters.depth: Batch adsorption: mass balance q = (C0 - Ce)V/W. Fixed bed: feed, mass-transfer zone, saturated zone, breakthrough at C/C0 set by rule (often 0.05), exhaustion at C/C0 near 0.95. Define breakthrough curve and length of unused bed. Use simple capacity by integrating (C0 - C)Q dt. Mention stagewise and moving-bed adsorbers as names some syllabi use. Keep isotherms to 6.2.

figure.title: Breakthrough curve
figure.aria: An S-shaped breakthrough curve rising slowly to C/C0 about 0.05 at 30 min, then steeply to 0.95 at 90 min.

chapters.example: A column contains 1.5 kg adsorbent. Feed is 80 mg/L at 2 L/min. Breakthrough (C/C0 = 0.05) is at 30 min; exhaustion (C/C0 = 0.95) is at 90 min. Assume exit concentration is negligible up to breakthrough. Find q at breakthrough in mg/g, and the fraction of bed capacity unused at breakthrough if capacity at exhaustion is used. q_b = 80 × 2 × 30 ÷ 1500 = 3.2 mg/g. q_exh = 80 × 2 × 90 ÷ 1500 = 9.6 mg/g. Unused fraction = (9.6 - 3.2) ÷ 9.6 = 0.667.
chapters.trap: Using exhaustion time in the breakthrough capacity, or treating C/C0 = 0.05 as exactly zero without saying so.
chapters.prereq: 6.1-6.2 adsorption and isotherms; Unit 2 mass transfer coefficients.
chapters.leave: Ion-exchange columns to 6.4; membrane permeate curves to 6.9.

chapters.idea: Ion exchange replaces one ionic species in solution with another held on a resin, without changing the total charge.
chapters.depth: Cation and anion resins; strong and weak acid/base resins; exchange capacity in eq/L or meq/g; selectivity; service, backwash, regeneration, rinse cycle. Equipment: fixed-bed columns, mixed-bed, counter-current regeneration. Applications: water softening, demineralisation, deionisation; some syllabi add chromatographic separations.

figure.title: Ion-exchange cycle
figure.aria: A downward cycle from service to exhaustion, backwash, regeneration and rinse, then back to service; regeneration is highlighted.

chapters.example: A cation resin has exchange capacity 1.2 eq/L. Feed is 500 L/h with 4 meq/L Ca²⁺. Find resin volume for an 8 h run. Total equivalents = 500 L/h × 8 h × 0.004 eq/L = 16 eq. Volume = 16 eq ÷ 1.2 eq/L = 13.3 L.
chapters.trap: Using mg/L as meq/L, or forgetting that 1 eq = 1000 meq.
chapters.prereq: 6.1 adsorption on solids; Unit 2 interphase transfer.
chapters.leave: Membrane ion removal to 6.9; crystallization to 6.5-6.8.

chapters.idea: A solution can hold more solute than its equilibrium solubility; that supersaturation is the driving force for crystallization.
chapters.depth: Solubility curves, temperature dependence, hydrates, polymorphs in brief, saturation, supersaturation ratio S = C/C* and relative supersaturation σ = (C - C*)/C*. Types of crystals; solid-liquid phase equilibrium; yield by mass balance from initial to final saturation. Mention cooling, evaporative and salting-out supersaturation. Keep nucleation and growth to 6.6.

figure.title: Solubility and cooling
figure.aria: A rising solubility curve from 20 g per 100 g water at 20 °C to 40 g at 60 °C; feed and final points sit on the curve, and the area above it is supersaturated.

chapters.example: A salt has solubility 40 g per 100 g water at 60 °C and 20 g per 100 g water at 20 °C. 1000 kg of saturated solution at 60 °C is cooled to 20 °C with no evaporation. Find crystals formed and yield based on original solute. At 60 °C: water = 1000 × 100/140 = 714.3 kg; solute = 285.7 kg. At 20 °C: solute held = 714.3 × 20/100 = 142.9 kg. Crystals = 285.7 - 142.9 = 142.9 kg. Yield = 142.9 ÷ 285.7 = 0.50, or 50%.
chapters.trap: Using g solute per 100 g solution instead of per 100 g water, or omitting water in the mass balance.
chapters.prereq: Unit 4 phase equilibrium ideas; 6.1-6.4 separation context.
chapters.leave: Nucleation and growth to 6.6; crystallizer heat duty to 6.7; CSD to 6.8.

chapters.idea: Supersaturation creates both new nuclei and growth of existing crystals; the balance between the two sets crystal number and size.
chapters.depth: Primary homogeneous and heterogeneous nucleation, secondary nucleation, critical nucleus, nucleation rate B = k_n S^n or B = k_n σ^n; growth rate G = k_g S^g; surface integration and diffusion growth. Factors: supersaturation, temperature, agitation, impurities, seeds. Some syllabi call σ the relative supersaturation. Keep population balance to 6.8.

figure.aria: A tree from supersaturation to nucleation and growth; nucleation splits into primary and secondary, primary into homogeneous and heterogeneous, and growth into diffusion and surface integration.

chapters.example: For a salt, G = k_g S^g with k_g = 5.0×10⁻⁵ m/s and g = 1.5. At S = 0.04, find G. By what factor must S rise to double G? G = 5.0×10⁻⁵ × (0.04)^1.5 = 5.0×10⁻⁵ × 0.008 = 4.0×10⁻⁷ m/s. For double G, S_new = 0.04 × 2^(1/1.5) = 0.0635, a factor 1.59.
chapters.trap: Using S = C - C* as a ratio, or applying the growth exponent to the relative supersaturation without saying which definition is used.
chapters.leave: Crystallizer classification and heat to 6.7; CSD to 6.8.

chapters.idea: Crystallizers are classified by how they create supersaturation and remove heat, and their yield follows a solute balance plus a heat balance.
chapters.depth: Classification: batch and continuous; cooling, evaporative, vacuum, reaction, salting-out; tank, Swenson-Walker, forced-circulation, draft-tube-baffle, Oslo. Yield and purity: mass balance with solubility, mother liquor, hydrates; heat effects: sensible cooling, latent heat of evaporation, heat of crystallization. Design considerations for batch and continuous: residence time, supersaturation control, heat-transfer area.

figure.aria: A classification tree of crystallizers into cooling, evaporative and reaction types, with one or two common examples under each branch.

chapters.example: 1000 kg/h feed contains 30 mass% solute at 50 °C and is cooled to 20 °C. Solubility at 20 °C is 20 g solute per 100 g water. cp of feed solution is 3.8 kJ/(kg K), heat of crystallization is 120 kJ/kg crystals, cooling water ΔT is 10 K and cp is 4.18 kJ/(kg K). Find crystals and cooling water. Feed: solute 300 kg/h, water 700 kg/h. At 20 °C: dissolved solute = 700 × 20/100 = 140 kg/h. Crystals = 300 - 140 = 160 kg/h. Sensible heat = 1000 × 3.8 × 30 = 114000 kJ/h. Crystallization heat = 160 × 120 = 19200 kJ/h. Total = 133200 kJ/h. Cooling water = 133200 ÷ (4.18 × 10) = 3.19×10³ kg/h.
chapters.trap: Using the feed mass as water in the solubility step, or forgetting the heat of crystallization.
chapters.leave: CSD and MSMPR to 6.8; membrane dewatering to 6.9.

chapters.idea: The crystal size distribution of a continuous mixed-suspension mixed-product-removal crystallizer follows an exponential population density curve set by growth rate and residence time.
chapters.depth: Define population density n, size L, residence time τ = V/Q, growth rate G. MSMPR assumptions: perfect mixing, constant volume, no classification, size-independent growth. n = n° exp(-L/(Gτ)); ln n vs L is a straight line with slope -1/(Gτ). Use to find n°, G, τ, and nucleation rate B = n°G with units stated. Mention CSD, dominant size, and design of batch and continuous crystallizers. Some syllabi call this population balance.

figure.title: MSMPR population density
figure.aria: A falling exponential population density from 2×10⁸ at zero size, with the worked point at L = 1 mm and n = 7.36×10⁷.

chapters.example: An MSMPR crystallizer has τ = 5 h, G = 0.20 mm/h, and n° = 2.0×10⁸ nuclei per m³ per mm. Find n at L = 1.0 mm and the slope of ln n vs L. n = 2.0×10⁸ × exp[-1.0 ÷ (0.20 × 5)] = 2.0×10⁸ × exp(-1) = 7.36×10⁷ per m³ per mm. Slope = -1 ÷ (Gτ) = -1 ÷ 1.0 = -1 mm⁻¹.
chapters.trap: Using τ in minutes with G in mm/h, or forgetting n° is the value at L = 0.
chapters.leave: Crystallizer heat duty to 6.7; membrane separations to 6.9.

chapters.idea: Membranes separate by letting some species pass and holding others back under a pressure or electric driving force.
chapters.depth: Osmosis and osmotic pressure; reverse osmosis for water desalination; ultrafiltration for macromolecules and colloids; electrodialysis with ion-exchange membranes and an electric field. Define flux J, rejection R = 1 - C_p/C_f, recovery = Q_p/Q_f. Some syllabi add solid and liquid membranes; only a few universities teach module design and concentration polarisation in detail.

figure.title: RO material balance
figure.aria: A reverse-osmosis flow from feed at 1000 L/h and 2000 mg/L through a high-pressure pump and module to permeate at 750 L/h and 100 mg/L and retentate at 250 L/h and 7700 mg/L.

chapters.example: An RO unit treats 1000 L/h feed with 2000 mg/L salt at 75% recovery. Permeate salt is 100 mg/L. Find permeate flow, retentate concentration and salt rejection. Permeate flow = 0.75 × 1000 = 750 L/h. Retentate flow = 250 L/h. Feed salt = 1000 × 2000 = 2.00×10⁶ mg/h. Permeate salt = 750 × 100 = 7.50×10⁴ mg/h. Retentate salt = 1.925×10⁶ mg/h; concentration = 1.925×10⁶ ÷ 250 = 7700 mg/L. Rejection = (1 - 100/2000) × 100 = 95%.
chapters.trap: Using recovery as the fraction retained, or applying rejection to the retentate instead of the permeate.
chapters.leave: Adsorption and ion exchange to 6.1-6.4; crystallization to 6.5-6.8.

links: adsorbent capacity leads to isotherm constants
fixed-bed mass balance carries over to ion-exchange columns
ion exchange and electrodialysis both remove ions
nucleation and growth set crystallizer duty and type
residence time and growth set the MSMPR size distribution
